# BarFlow

> Fast Python progress-bar library with a C++ core. Cross-platform: Windows, macOS, Linux.
> `barflow.track()` wraps an iterable in a live bar whose hot path is a
> single atomic `fetch_add` in C++ plus the CPython call trampoline. A
> background render thread owns all formatting and I/O, so the producer
> loop never pays for rendering inline. Beats tqdm, rich.progress, and
> alive-progress simultaneously on cold-import time, per-iter overhead,
> peak it/s, and CPU cost (see benchmarks).

This file follows the [llmstxt.org](https://llmstxt.org/) convention so
AI assistants working inside this repo can orient themselves quickly.
Links are repo-relative paths — every entry is a real file you can open
with your file tool.

## What BarFlow is

BarFlow is a single PyPI distribution (`barflow`) that ships a compiled
C-extension module (`barflow._core`, built from `src/barflow/_core.cpp`)
plus a thin Python package that layers column factories, themes,
spinners, hooks, and an asyncio wrapper on top. The top-level import is
kept deliberately tiny (~2 ms) via `__getattr__` lazy-loading of every
non-hot-path submodule.

Key public API (see `src/barflow/__init__.py` for the full surface):

- `barflow.track(iterable, total=None, desc=None, *, columns=None,
  theme=None, task_id=0, disable=False, min_interval=0.05,
  capture_output=False)` — the fast-path iterator wrapper. Returns a
  C-level `Tracker`. Fast path (no columns/theme/capture) goes
  straight to `_core.Progress`; decorated calls route through the
  Python `Progress` subclass in `_progress.py`.
- `barflow.Progress(*columns, total=None, desc=None, theme=None,
  disable=False, min_interval=0.05, capture_output=False)` — context
  manager for manual `tick()` / `advance()` / `add_task()` / `update()`
  / `write_above()` / `pause()` / `resume()` flows. Resolves columns +
  themes in Python, then
  calls into `_core.Progress`.
- `barflow.Tracker` — the C iterator type, re-exported for advanced use.
- `barflow.aio.atrack(aiter, ...)` — async-iterable wrapper.

## Python source (`src/barflow/`)

- [src/barflow/\_\_init\_\_.py](src/barflow/__init__.py): Package entry
  point. Defines `track()` and the `__getattr__` hook that lazy-loads
  `Progress`, `columns`, `themes`, `spinners`, `aio`, and `hooks`.
- [src/barflow/\_progress.py](src/barflow/_progress.py): Python
  `Progress` subclass of `_core.Progress`. Resolves columns/themes and
  wires up `capture_output=True` via `hooks.StdoutCapture`.
- [src/barflow/columns.py](src/barflow/columns.py): Column factories —
  `TextColumn`, `DescriptionColumn`, `BarColumn`, `PercentColumn`,
  `CountColumn`, `RateColumn`, `ElapsedColumn`, `EtaColumn`,
  `SpinnerColumn`, and `CallbackColumn` (the last accepts a Python
  callable rendered on the column pipeline) — plus `resolve_columns()`
  which converts Python column objects into the 5-tuple the C core
  expects.
- [src/barflow/themes.py](src/barflow/themes.py): Named presets
  (`classic`, `fire`, `neon`, `cyberpunk`, …) — each is a pre-built
  list of columns you can pass via `theme="..."`.
- [src/barflow/bar\_styles.py](src/barflow/bar_styles.py): Glyph sets
  for `BarColumn(glyphs=...)` — blocks, ASCII, shades, pipes, etc.
- [src/barflow/spinners.py](src/barflow/spinners.py): Spinner frame
  library and the compositional DSL (`frame`, `scrolling`, `bouncing`,
  `alongside`, `sequential`). Spinners are materialized into flat
  string lists at build time so the render thread does `frames[tick %
  len]` with no Python-side cost.
- [src/barflow/style.py](src/barflow/style.py): ANSI color/style parser
  used by every column that takes a `color=`/`style=` argument.
- [src/barflow/hooks.py](src/barflow/hooks.py): `StdoutCapture` — the
  `print()` interception that routes writes through
  `Progress.write_above()` so user prints appear above live bars
  without tearing.
- [src/barflow/aio.py](src/barflow/aio.py): `atrack()` — asyncio
  wrapper around an async iterable.

## C++ core

- [src/barflow/\_core.cpp](src/barflow/_core.cpp): The entire C
  extension in one file (~2,170 lines). Contains:
  - `Task` struct (atomic counter, total, desc, start time).
  - `Progress` type (vector of tasks, render mutex + cv, column
    pipeline, ANSI bar rendering with 1/8-block partial cells).
  - `Tracker` type — a PyObject with a custom `tp_iternext` that does
    `PyIter_Next(inner)` then `fetch_add(&task->count, 1,
    memory_order_relaxed)`.
  - Render thread: wakes on cv timeout (default 50 ms), snapshots all
    task counts, runs the column pipeline, writes to stderr via
    `WriteConsoleW` (Windows, UTF-16 transcoded, 32 KB chunks) or
    `write(2)` (POSIX).
  - `write_above()` primitive for interleaving user prints.
  - `pause()` / `resume()` to suspend the render thread and clear the
    bar area so an external writer (e.g. an output redirector) can emit
    lines without the autonomous render thread tearing them, then
    repaint. `pause()` checks `vt_enabled` before erasing.
  - Ten built-in column types decoded from Python 5-tuples: `TEXT`,
    `DESCRIPTION`, `BAR`, `PERCENT`, `COUNT`, `RATE`, `ELAPSED`, `ETA`,
    `SPINNER`, `CALLBACK`. Only `CALLBACK` re-enters Python on the
    render thread; the other nine are pure C++.

## Documentation

- [docs/DESIGN.md](docs/DESIGN.md): Full architecture writeup — the
  three-axis goal (startup, peak it/s, display-on throughput), hot-path
  design, render thread, column pipeline, Windows console handling,
  memory model, and the rationale behind each design choice. Start
  here if you're changing the core.
- [docs/FEATURE\_REQUESTS.md](docs/FEATURE_REQUESTS.md): Backlog sourced
  from open issues across tqdm, rich, and alive-progress — features
  users have asked for that BarFlow doesn't yet ship. Ordered by
  rough priority.
- [docs/PUBLISHING.md](docs/PUBLISHING.md): One-time PyPI setup and the
  per-release checklist. Covers `build_dist.bat`, cibuildwheel wheel
  matrix, and the `gh release` trigger.

## Examples (`examples/`)

- [examples/showcase.py](examples/showcase.py): Seven-scenario demo —
  simple `track()`, custom columns, named themes, multi-task, captured
  prints, etc. Works from any cwd. Good to run after a code change to
  eyeball visual output.
- [examples/themes\_showcase.py](examples/themes_showcase.py): Theme
  gallery — runs every named theme in sequence. Supports
  `--only <name>...` to filter.
- [examples/parallel\_presets.py](examples/parallel_presets.py):
  Multi-thread demo — one `Progress` instance per preset, one worker
  thread per preset, shared cursor via ANSI cursor-up. Exercises the
  render-mutex + `last_rendered_lines` accounting.
- [examples/async\_stream.py](examples/async_stream.py): `barflow.aio`
  demo — pulsing indeterminate bar over an async iterable with unknown
  total.

## Benchmarks

- [benchmarks/bench.py](benchmarks/bench.py): Main harness that measures
  (1) cold import startup via subprocess with baseline subtraction,
  (2) no-display hot path it/s, (3) display-on it/s against an
  `io.StringIO` sink with `force_terminal=True`, and (4) CPU cost via
  `time.process_time()` (which sums all threads — the background
  render thread cannot hide). Run:
  `python benchmarks/bench.py --n 20000000 --runs 5`.
- [benchmarks/bench\_raw.md](benchmarks/bench_raw.md): Latest raw
  output from the harness — regenerated every time `bench.py` runs.
- [benchmarks/results.md](benchmarks/results.md): Methodology and
  platform notes. Explains why tqdm is run with `mininterval=0.05`
  (matching barflow's default) rather than the out-of-box 0.10.
- Specialized microbench scripts — `bench_first_frame.py`,
  `bench_memory.py`, `bench_metadata_churn.py`, `bench_multibar.py`,
  `bench_tail_latency.py` — each isolates one axis (first-frame
  latency, RSS, metadata update cost, multi-task fan-out, tail
  latency). Useful for regression-hunting a specific code path.
- [README.md](README.md#benchmarks): Headline table + per-axis
  breakdown. At N = 20 M iters on Windows 11 / Python 3.13: barflow
  wins cold import by 15–28×, per-iter overhead by 2.2×, display-on
  throughput by 4.9× vs tqdm, and burns ~5× less CPU than tqdm /
  ~50× less than rich and alive-progress.

## Build & packaging

- [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml): `setuptools` build backend,
  metadata, classifiers, keyword list, PEP 639 SPDX license field.
  Build dependencies are just `setuptools>=77` + `wheel`.
- [setup.py](setup.py): Declares the `barflow._core` extension with
  the C++ source, language standard, and per-platform compile flags.
- [MANIFEST.in](MANIFEST.in): Sdist inclusion rules.
- [build.bat](build.bat): One-shot local build for dev work on
  Windows (`python -m pip install -e .` with the MSVC toolchain).
- [build\_dist.bat](build_dist.bat): Builds sdist + the local-platform
  wheel into `dist/`. Full wheel matrix is produced by cibuildwheel in
  CI, not by this script.
- [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md): Keep-a-Changelog-style release notes.
  The `Build wheels` workflow extracts the section for the pushed tag
  via `.github/scripts/extract_changelog.py` and uses it as the body
  of the GitHub release.
- [LICENSE](LICENSE): MIT.

## Performance tips & best practices

Rules grounded in the actual implementation — if you break them the
benchmarks will catch you. The first group targets users of barflow,
the second targets anyone touching the C core.

### For users

- **Prefer `track()` over a manual `Progress` context when you can.**
  `track()` has a fast path (see `src/barflow/__init__.py:31`): if
  you pass no `columns`, no `theme`, and `capture_output=False`, it
  skips the Python `Progress` subclass entirely and instantiates
  `_core.Progress` directly — one C construction, zero Python-side
  column resolution. Adding a `theme=` or custom columns forces the
  slow path through `_progress.Progress` which is still fast but
  does extra Python work at setup time.
- **Keep `min_interval` at the default (50 ms).** The render thread
  sleeps on a condition variable with this timeout; at 20 fps you
  get smooth motion without paying for renders the user can't see.
  Lowering it below ~20 ms mostly burns CPU on re-renders that look
  identical. Raising it above ~100 ms starts to feel laggy but
  drops render-thread CPU toward zero — useful for long-running
  background jobs where the bar is a liveness check, not a UX
  element.
- **Reuse one `Progress` across many tasks.** A single `Progress`
  instance has one render thread, one render mutex, and one column
  pipeline — add tasks to it with `add_task(total, desc)` instead
  of spinning up a fresh `Progress` per task. The render thread
  already walks every task on each tick.
- **Don't pass `capture_output=True` unless you need it.** It wires
  `hooks.StdoutCapture` in front of `sys.stdout` / `sys.stderr` so
  any `print()` calls route through `Progress.write_above()`. That
  adds a Python-level write interceptor on every user print — fine
  for interactive scripts, unnecessary overhead for batch jobs
  where you aren't printing from inside the loop.
- **Use `disable=True` in tests or non-TTY runs.** It suppresses all
  rendering and I/O: `__enter__` returns early without starting the
  render thread, and `write_bytes` becomes a no-op. The per-iteration
  counter still updates, though — `tick`/`advance`/`Tracker` always run
  the relaxed atomic `fetch_add`; there is no `disable` short-circuit in
  the hot path, so it does not drop to a single comparison.
- **Avoid `CallbackColumn` in tight loops unless you need it.** It's
  the only built-in column type that re-enters Python on the render
  thread. The render thread acquires the GIL once per frame to run
  callback columns (see `render_frame` around `_core.cpp:889`), but
  if your callback is expensive or allocates heavily, it can
  dominate render-thread cost and delay the next frame. Move the
  computation out of the column if you can.
- **For unknown totals (generators), theme accordingly.** Columns
  that need a total (`PercentColumn`, `EtaColumn`) render empty when
  `total=0`. Use a theme that only shows a spinner + rate +
  elapsed, or build one manually with just `SpinnerColumn` +
  `CountColumn` + `RateColumn`.
- **Free-threaded builds.** `cp314t` wheels exist on PyPI
  (`cp313t` was dropped after 0.5.1). On a no-GIL interpreter,
  `Tracker.tp_iternext` still does the same atomic `fetch_add`, and
  producer threads scale almost linearly across cores because the
  hot path never acquires a lock. The render thread is still
  single-threaded.

### For contributors touching `_core.cpp`

- **The producer cacheline is sacred.** `Task.completed` is
  `alignas(kCacheLine) std::atomic<uint64_t>` followed by an
  explicit pad (`_core.cpp:212-218`). Cold fields (total, desc,
  start time) live on a different line, so a `fetch_add` from the
  producer core doesn't bounce the description string back and
  forth. Don't add new hot fields to `Task` without putting them
  next to `completed` and extending the pad.
- **`fetch_add` uses `memory_order_relaxed`.** Never upgrade it
  without a benchmark showing the old ordering was actually wrong.
  The render thread reads `completed` with `memory_order_acquire`
  (`_core.cpp:1037, 1322`) which is enough for our "the renderer
  sees a monotonically non-decreasing count" guarantee. We don't
  need release semantics on the producer side because we aren't
  publishing any other state through the counter.
- **Column formatting belongs on the render thread, not the
  producer.** Every column type except `CALLBACK` is rendered from
  pure C++ state; the producer loop has zero column-aware work.
  If you find yourself threading column state through
  `advance()`, stop — move it to `render_frame`.
- **Gate `render_cv.notify_one()`.** Calling `notify_one` on every
  `advance` is a perf trap: even when no waiter is parked, the cv
  still acquires its internal mutex. The hot path should only
  notify when it has crossed a render threshold. Watch the dirty
  counter pattern in `render_frame` / `render_loop`
  (`_core.cpp:1302-1328`) before adding notifications elsewhere.
- **The render thread drops the GIL around `render_frame`.** See
  the comment at `_core.cpp:1843-1844`: the render loop releases
  GIL before painting so that `CallbackColumn` implementations
  (and user code that acquires the GIL via `write_above()`) can
  re-acquire it via `PyGILState_Ensure` without deadlocking. If
  you add a new render-thread entry point, follow the same
  convention.
- **Benchmark before merging.** `python benchmarks/bench.py --n
  5000000 --runs 3` is the quick check. If `track()` drops below
  ~95 M it/s on Windows / Python 3.13, investigate before pushing
  further changes. Full `--n 20000000 --runs 5` run is reserved
  for the final pass of each iteration (see `ITERATIONS.md`).
- **Don't change the column tuple shape without version-gating it.**
  `parse_columns` currently accepts 5-tuple *or* 6-tuple rows so
  that pre-glyph user code still works. Any further schema change
  needs the same kind of tolerant parse, otherwise you break every
  user who cached a theme dict.

## Optional

- [ITERATIONS.md](ITERATIONS.md): Running log of design iterations and
  micro-benchmarks collected while tuning the hot path. Historical —
  not needed for day-to-day work, but useful if you want context on
  why a particular optimization is shaped the way it is.
- [.github/](.github/): GitHub Actions workflows (cibuildwheel matrix,
  PyPI publish via Trusted Publisher, automatic GitHub release on tag
  with wheels attached) plus `scripts/extract_changelog.py` which
  pulls the per-tag section out of `CHANGELOG.md` for the release
  body.
